prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art text-to-video generation relies heavily on computationally expensive training or specific architectural modifications to pre-trained image models. Existing "zero-shot" or "training-free" methods are often brittle; they depend on manipulating specific internal modules (such as cross-attention maps in U-Nets). This lack of flexibility means that when image generation architectures evolve (e.g., shifting from U-Nets to Transformers), previous video generation techniques become obsolete. We aim to address the need for a universally compatible, model-agnostic framework that can generate temporally coherent video from *any* off-the-shelf image diffusion model without requiring access to internal weights or additional training.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can synthesize motion and maintain temporal coherence solely by manipulating the **intersection of diffusion trajectories** in the latent space.

Our core intuition relies on the deterministic nature of ODE-based diffusion. We postulate that by initiating a denoising trajectory with one prompt (Frame $A$) and "switching" to a different prompt (Frame $B$) at a specific timestep, we can control the deviation between the two frames. An earlier switch allows for high variance (motion), while a later switch forces high coherence (static background). We believe that applying this switching mechanism spatially—via a grid rather than globally—will allow us to simulate realistic motion by ensuring that moving objects diverge from the previous frame's trajectory earlier than the static background.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a pipeline ("EIDT-V") that operates entirely on the inputs and outputs of the diffusion process (latents and prompts), treating the model itself as a black box.

**1. Semantic Planning via LLMs**
We will utilize a Large Language Model (LLM) as a "director" to generate two text-based streams:
*   **Frame-wise Prompts:** A sequence of prompts where a fixed scene descriptor ensures continuity, and a dynamic component describes the specific action for each frame.
*   **Difference Detection:** A parallel process that compares the prompts of consecutive frames to textually identify *what* is changing (e.g., "arm waving," "clouds moving").

**2. Spatial Localization via CLIP Attention**
To map the textual differences to specific regions in the image, we will employ a CLIP-based segmentation or attention module. By comparing the "difference text" against the current image state, we will generate an attention map that highlights regions requiring motion.

**3. Grid-Based Prompt Switching Strategy**
This is the core of our technical novelty. Instead of applying a global prompt change, we will divide the latent image into a spatial grid. We will define a **Switch Time Matrix** derived from the attention map:
*   **High Attention Areas (Motion):** Assigned an "early" switch time. These grid cells will switch to the Frame $B$ trajectory early in the denoising process, allowing the model to generate new content/poses.
*   **Low Attention Areas (Static):** Assigned a "late" switch time. These cells will follow the Frame $A$ trajectory for most of the process, ensuring the background remains structurally identical to the previous frame.

**4. Latent Composition**
During the sampling loop, we will dynamically assemble the latent vector at each timestep. Based on the current time and the Switch Time Matrix, we will use a binary mask to select whether a specific grid cell draws its value from the original trajectory or the new prompt's trajectory. This effectively blends "generation" (for moving parts) and "reconstruction" (for static parts) seamlessly in the latent space.

## Expected Contribution
We anticipate this research will establish a robust baseline for **model-agnostic video generation**. By abstracting the control mechanism away from specific network layers (like self-attention) and focusing on latent trajectory intersections, our approach should theoretically work out-of-the-box with any future image diffusion architecture (including SDXL, SD3, or Flux). This creates a scalable, low-cost path for video synthesis that preserves the high visual fidelity of foundational image models while ensuring temporal consistency without training.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a series of experiments to evaluate a model-agnostic, zero-shot, training-free text-to-video generation pipeline (EIDT-V). The system operates by exploiting intersections in diffusion trajectories and utilizing grid-based prompt switching.

*   **Hardware and Compute:** All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU (24 GB memory).
*   **Datasets:** We created a custom evaluation set consisting of 50 diverse video generation prompts selected to span various visual and semantic contexts.
*   **Core Image Models:**
    *   Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) - primarily used for fair comparison with baselines.
    *   Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) - used to test adaptability.
    *   Stable Diffusion 3 Medium (SD3 Medium) - used to test adaptability and scalability.
    *   IP-Adapter - tested as a modular alternative to cross-attention manipulation.
*   **Auxiliary Models:**
    *   **LLM:** LLaMA-3 8B was used for in-context learning to generate framewise conditional text prompts and to detect differences between frames.
    *   **Segmentation:** A CLIP-Segmentation model was used to create attention maps for the switch time matrix (STM).
    *   **Token Limits:** We allocated 60 tokens for the fixed scene descriptor and 15 tokens for the dynamic component (with a 2-token buffer) to fit within CLIP's 77-token limit.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **MS-SSIM (Multi-Scale Structural Similarity):** Quantifies structural similarity between consecutive frames (Higher is better).
    *   **LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity):** Assesses perceptual similarity via deep features (Lower is better).
    *   **Temporal Consistency Loss:** Optical Flow-based metric using the Farneback method to evaluate motion consistency (Lower is better).
    *   **User Study:** Human ranking (1-4 scale) on Temporal Coherence, Fidelity, Semantic Coherence, and Overall Score.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   T2V-Zero (based on SD1.5)
    *   DirecT2V (based on SD1.5)
    *   Free-Bloom (based on SD1.5)

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Quantitative Performance Comparison of Video Generation Models**
*Note: This table compares baseline methods against our method (EIDT-V) across multiple configurations and architectures. Standard deviations are included.*

| Method | Pre-Trained Model | Unmodified Architecture? | MS-SSIM (↑) | LPIPS (↓) | Temporal Consistency (↓) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| T2V-Zero | SD1.5 | No | 0.428 ± 0.174 | 0.404 ± 0.083 | 0.206 ± 0.066 |
| DirecT2V | SD1.5 | No | 0.492 ± 0.135 | 0.445 ± 0.089 | 0.185 ± 0.061 |
| Free-Bloom | SD1.5 | No | 0.672 ± 0.095 | 0.353 ± 0.082 | 0.159 ± 0.039 |
| **EIDT-V (Ours)** | **SD1.5** | **Yes** | **0.630 ± 0.137** | **0.330 ± 0.100** | **0.152 ± 0.062** |
| EIDT-V (Ours) | SD1.5 w/ IP-Adapter | No | 0.655 ± 0.130 | 0.316 ± 0.089 | 0.158 ± 0.074 |
| EIDT-V (Ours) | SDXL | Yes | 0.701 ± 0.089 | 0.280 ± 0.086 | 0.138 ± 0.054 |
| EIDT-V (Ours) | SD3 Medium | Yes | 0.810 ± 0.109 | 0.184 ± 0.080 | 0.087 ± 0.042 |

**Table 2: User Study Results**
*Note: Scores represent mean ranking out of 4. Lower scores indicate better performance.*

| Method | Temporal Coherence (↓) | Fidelity (↓) | Semantic Coherence (↓) | Overall (↓) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| FreeBloom | 2.5 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 2.3 |
| T2VZero | 2.4 | 2.5 | 2.7 | 2.5 |
| DirecT2V | 3.2 | 3.5 | 3.1 | 3.3 |
| **EIDT-V (Ours)** | **1.9** | **2.0** | **2.1** | **1.9** |

**Table 3: Ablation Study Results**
*Note: Evaluates components: ChatGPT Prompts (CG), Our Framewise Prompts (OFP), and Grid Prompt Switching (GrPS).*

| Configuration | MS-SSIM (↑) | LPIPS (↓) | Temp. Cons. (↓) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CG | 0.132 ± 0.052 | 0.723 ± 0.043 | 0.389 ± 0.046 |
| OFP | 0.124 ± 0.082 | 0.686 ± 0.062 | 0.403 ± 0.078 |
| CG + GrPS | 0.588 ± 0.129 | 0.384 ± 0.094 | 0.157 ± 0.062 |
| **OFP + GrPS** | **0.630 ± 0.137** | **0.330 ± 0.100** | **0.152 ± 0.062** |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Methodological Observations**
*   We found that utilizing intersections of trajectories alone working only with latent values was insufficient to obtain localized frame-wise coherence and diversity.
*   We observed that earlier switching times in the grid-based approach resulted in higher variance, while later switching resulted in greater coherence. This confirmed the ability to control the balance between coherence and variance.
*   We noted that significant prompt changes late in the diffusion process occasionally prevented the full refinement of fine details.

**Visual Comparison with Baselines (SD1.5 Architecture)**
*   **Prompt: "A chameleon changing colors on a branch"**
    *   *T2V-Zero:* Produced coherent frames but failed to execute the prompt specific; the chameleon did not change colors.
    *   *DirecT2V:* Struggled to generate coherent frames.
    *   *Free-Bloom:* Captured the essence of the animal but failed to integrate color changes temporally.
    *   *EIDT-V:* Successfully demonstrated clear color changes in the chameleon while keeping the rest of the frame consistent.
*   **Prompt: "A horse galloping across a field"**
    *   *EIDT-V:* Effectively captured the horse's movement, specifically leg positioning, demonstrating temporal motion accuracy.
*   **Prompt: "An astronaut floating in space waving"**
    *   *T2V-Zero:* The astronaut did not appear to be waving.
    *   *LLM-based Baselines (DirecT2V/Free-Bloom):* Captured the semantic concepts of "waving" and "space" but failed to integrate them into each frame consistently.
    *   *EIDT-V:* Showed the astronaut's arm moving in a waving pattern while maintaining high consistency in the background and subject.

**Cross-Architecture Observations**
*   **SDXL Implementation:** Produced frames with improved clarity and detail compared to the SD1.5 implementation.
*   **SD3 Medium Implementation:** Further enhanced performance, achieving the highest visual fidelity and the lowest temporal consistency loss, significantly reducing flickering artifacts.

**Ablation Qualitative Analysis (Prompt: "A cup of coffee being poured with steam rising")**
*   **Naive Approach (No Grid Prompt Switching, No OFP):** Produced images linked only by theme, lacking temporal continuity.
*   **OFP without GrPS:** Offered only minor improvements over the naive approach.
*   **CG with GrPS:** Notably increased coherence compared to non-GrPS configurations.
*   **OFP + GrPS (Full Method):** Yielded the best performance with smooth transitions and high stability.

**User Study Feedback**
*   Participants noted that EIDT-V produced smoother videos with a focus on coherence.
*   Participants observed that the baseline FreeBloom focused more on text alignment than temporal coherence.
*   EIDT-V was rated as having superior visual quality with fewer artifacts than comparison models.

[AVAILABLE FIGURES]
### AVAILABLE FIGURES LIST

  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of different video generation models across three prompts: (a) “A chameleon changing colors on a branch”, (b) “A horse galloping across a field”, and (c) “An astronaut floating in space waving”. T2VZero produces coherent frames but does not fully capture the specifics of each prompt; for instance, the chameleon does not change colors, and the astronaut does not appear to be waving. DirecT2V struggles to generate coherent frames. Interestingly, both DirecT2V and FreeBloom, which are LLM-based models, capture the essence of “waving” and ”space” but fail to fully integrate these concepts in each frame. They have strong semantic coherence but not temporal. Our model, however, demonstrates clear color changes in the chameleon, captures the horse’s movement (notice the legs), and shows the astronaut’s arm moving in a waving pattern while keeping the rest of the frame highly consistent.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 2:
  - Filename: figure_1.png
  - Caption: Figure 1. EIDT-V Pipeline for Frame-Based Video Generation. The pipeline consists of two primary modules: text and video. The text module converts the user’s input into framewise prompts and expected variations, which guide the video module in generating frames iteratively. The video module achieves controlled variance and coherence across frames by leveraging trajectory intersections. Integrating two LLM modules and the grid prompt switching enables a generic image diffusion model to synthesize coherent video sequences effectively.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Grid Prompt Switching with Text-Guided Attention. On the right, an auxiliary block processes the previous frame and difference text using a CLIP segmentation model to generate the STM. This is converted into a binary mask (Eq. (4)) that selects, at timestep t, whether each grid cell follows the original or new prompt trajectory. In the main denoising process, the mask blends the latent representations X (A) t and X (B)
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4. Ablation Qualitative Results (see Tab. 3). Each row displays four equally spaced frames from the generated GIF. The prompt is “A cup of coffee being poured with steam rising”. The naive approach produces images linked only by theme. Applying OFP without GrPS offers minor improvements while incorporating GrPS (CG with GrPS) notably increases coherence. Finally, combining OFP with GrPS yields the best performance.
--------------------------------------------------

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Recent advancements in generative AI have produced powerful image diffusion models; however, extending these capabilities to video generation remains a significant technical bottleneck. State-of-the-art video models (e.g., Sora, MovieGen) rely on massive computational resources, extensive training datasets, and complex, inaccessible architectures. Conversely, existing "low-cost" or zero-shot approaches often require specific architectural modifications to the underlying image model (such as manipulating specific attention layers), which limits their flexibility and renders them obsolete as soon as the base model architecture evolves (e.g., moving from UNet to Transformers).

There is currently no robust method to transform a pre-trained, text-to-image diffusion model into a video generator that is effectively **model-agnostic**, **training-free**, and capable of maintaining high **temporal coherence** without modifying the internal weights or architecture of the base model.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose a novel framework, **EIDT-V (Exploiting Intersections in Diffusion Trajectories)**, to achieve zero-shot, training-free text-to-video generation.

Our core hypothesis is that we can control the trade-off between temporal coherence and motion variance entirely within the **latent space** by manipulating **diffusion trajectories**. We posit that by defining a specific "intersection point" in the denoising process—where the trajectory switches from a source frame's conditioning to a target frame's conditioning—we can mathematically bound the divergence between frames. Furthermore, by applying this switching mechanism spatially via a **grid-based mask** derived from cross-modal attention (CLIP), we can localize motion to specific semantic regions while freezing the background, thereby ensuring frame-to-frame consistency without additional training.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a pipeline that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) for prompt engineering with a grid-based trajectory intersection mechanism within the diffusion sampling loop. The methodology operates as follows:

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Diffusion Intersections
We treat the generation of consecutive frames as deterministic trajectories in latent space. Let a diffusion trajectory be defined by the Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) evolution of a latent $x$ from noise $x_T$ to data $x_0$, conditioned on prompt $y$.

We define two trajectories for consecutive frames:
1.  **Trajectory A:** Guided by prompt $y$ (current frame).
2.  **Trajectory B:** Guided by prompt $y'$ (next frame).

We will implement a **Prompt Switch**, where the denoising process follows Trajectory A until timestep $t = t_s$, and then switches to Trajectory B. This intersection at $t_s$ creates a dependency that constrains the maximum separation of the final outputs.

### 2. Grid-Based Prompt Switching
Global switching affects the entire image equally, which is insufficient for complex scenes where only specific objects should move. We will strictly define an $n \times n$ grid over the latent space.

We will define a **Switch Time Matrix (STM)**, where each cell $(i, j)$ in the grid is assigned a specific switch time $t_s^{(i, j)}$.
During the denoising steps $t \in [T, 0]$, we will generate a binary mask $M_t^{(i, j)}$ for each cell:

$$
M _ { t } ^ { ( i , j ) } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 , } & { \mathrm { if ~ } t > t _ { s } ^ { ( i , j ) } } \\ { 1 , } & { \mathrm { if ~ } t \leq t _ { s } ^ { ( i , j ) } } \end{array} \right.
$$

Here, a value of $0$ indicates the process follows the original trajectory (A), and $1$ indicates it follows the new trajectory (B).

The composite latent representation $X_t$ at any step $t$ will be calculated by blending the latents from both trajectories element-wise:

$$
X _ { t } = M _ { t } \odot X _ { t } ^ { ( B ) } + ( 1 - M _ { t } ) \odot X _ { t } ^ { ( A ) }
$$

Where:
*   $X_t^{(A)}$ is the latent state derived using prompt $y$.
*   $X_t^{(B)}$ is the latent state derived using prompt $y'$.
*   $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication.

### 3. Text-Guided Attention for STM Generation
To automate the creation of the STM, we will utilize a **CLIP-Segmentation based attention mechanism**.
1.  We will compute the textual difference $\Delta$ between the initial prompt $y$ and the target prompt $y'$.
2.  We will generate attention maps over the image $x_0^A$ using $\Delta$ to identify regions of high semantic change (motion).
3.  These attention maps will be normalized, exponentiated, and resized to the grid resolution to populate the STM.
    *   **High attention values** will result in **earlier switch times** (higher variance/motion).
    *   **Low attention values** will result in **later switch times** (higher coherence/stability).

### 4. LLM-Driven Prompt Engineering
To drive the trajectories, we will integrate two in-context learned modules using a Large Language Model (e.g., LLaMA):

*   **Module 1: Framewise Prompt Generator:**
    This module will generate a sequence of prompts $y_t$. We will enforce a strict token allocation structure to preserve context:
    $$
    y _ { t } = \mathrm { Fixed ~ Scene ~ Descriptor } + \mathrm { Dynamic ~ Component } _ { t }
    $$
    We will allocate approximately 60 tokens for the fixed descriptor (background/style) and 15 tokens for the dynamic component (motion), ensuring the embeddings remain consistent across the video.

*   **Module 2: Difference Detector:**
    This module will compare consecutive prompts to extract the difference list $\Delta$, which feeds into the CLIP-attention module described in Section 3.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Model Agnosticism:** This proposal outlines a method that operates purely on latents and prompts. It will function with Stable Diffusion 1.5, SDXL, SD3, or Flux without any code changes to the model architecture itself.
2.  **Precise Spatial Control:** By introducing the Grid-Based Prompt Switching and STM, we theoretically solve the problem of "global hallucination" in zero-shot video, allowing for localized motion while freezing the background.
3.  **Efficiency:** This approach eliminates the need for temporal attention modules or costly 3D-conv training, providing a computationally efficient pathway for high-quality video generation on consumer hardware.

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit.
